A Home with Two Keys:
Two people came to the district administration with documents for the same flat. The first, a schoolteacher from a mountain district, had left during the final bombardments and kept his pre-war registration booklet all that time. The second, a railwayman's widow with a child, had received the same flat from the emergency committee after her home burned down during the civil war.

Both documents were genuine. One bore the seal of Ivanov's administration, the other that of the resistance's military council. The clerk placed them side by side and asked which was now considered lawful. Several soldiers by the door proposed a simple solution: return the flat to its pre-war owner. Then the widow asked where she was supposed to return to.

Shabrat refused to turn victory into another eviction. The old right could not simply be declared void, but neither could the new republic begin by ordering a family onto the street. The administration was instructed to register both claims, leave the current occupants in place until alternative housing was provided, and recognise the returning owner's right to a new home or compensation.

There were more than one or even a hundred such cases. Steland was quickly discovering that rebuilding a country did not mean putting everything back as it had been. Sometimes it meant deciding, for the first time, what to do with two people who each held a genuine key.
Victory grants no right to someone else's door.

The queue outside the old army depot formed before dawn. Former resistance units brought rifles from Party arsenals, Kefreyt assault rifles, hunting carbines and crates of grenades which had spent years listed as flour, tools or nothing at all. Some weapons had their serial numbers filed off. That was how they had reached the mountains in the first place.

The commander of an old cell refused to surrender his rifle. He pointed out that the Party had also started with registers, then used those same lists to come for people at night. Several people in the queue silently agreed. A new uniform and a new seal did not automatically make the state someone they trusted with their weapons.

Shabrat unholstered his own pistol, removed the magazine and placed the weapon on the table before the clerk. His name became the first entry in the new register. He then signed an order: every armed detachment must either join the common army and accept a civilian chain of command, or surrender its heavy weapons and disband. There would be no separate army of the victors.

By evening, the queue had grown longer. Some left with duty orders, others with demobilisation papers. The resistance was handing the state the force that had once allowed it to survive. For the first time, it was doing so not because it had lost.
